name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 16 April 1977

blocks.note: surface reading: the drunken rapture of a reveller in the train of Bacchus, god of wine
setter's reading: wine-related, pointing at a word for a year's wine harvest, and transport is a motor vehicle

explanation.surface: Being carried away by wine, as a follower of Bacchus might be.
explanation.walkthrough: Transport suggests ecstasy; here it is a means of getting about. A vintage is a year's wine crop, which is why the car qualifies as Bacchic.
explanation.definitionFit: An old motor built in the 1920s is called by a term borrowed from wine vocabulary, so it is jokingly a wine god's vehicle.

blocks.note: an imp is a little demon
ale is a drink, beer

explanation.surface: A temperance cry: lace the evil liquor, or denounce it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spike' looks like adding alcohol to a drink; here it is the verb meaning to run through with a point.
explanation.definitionFit: To spike something is to pierce it on a sharp stake, exactly the sense of the verb in the grid.

indicators.note: a word misspelt has its letters set down in the wrong order, so the fodder must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a typesetter got the word shellback wrong, itself misspelt.
explanation.walkthrough: Shellback is normally slang for an old sailor; here it describes a creature with a shell on its back.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater turtle carries a hard shell on its back, so the whimsical compound describes it.

clue.text: Did a king of Phrygia show such moderation?

definitions.text: Did a king of Phrygia show such moderation?

blocks.clueFragment: Did a king of Phrygia show such moderation?
blocks.note: surface reading: a question about whether some ancient ruler was temperate
setter's reading: Midas, whose touch turned things to gold and who was famously greedy, so his moderation would be gilded and stingy

explanation.surface: A history question about the temperance of an ancient Phrygian monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Midas of Phrygia turned all he touched to gold; mean also means miserly, which suits his greed.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the Aristotelian ideal of a happy medium between extremes, which is moderation itself.

clue.text: Birds said to dress hair of sheep

indicators.note: said tells us the words that follow are to be heard spoken rather than read as spelt

blocks.note: to curl is to dress hair, and ewes are female sheep

explanation.surface: A claim that some birds groom the fleece of sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: These are long-billed wading birds with a haunting call, found on moors and shores.

blocks.note: first meaning: an old card game, a forerunner of whist
second meaning: a sandpiper whose males grow a frilled collar in breeding season

explanation.surface: An ageing game bird, perhaps a pheasant past its best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old game bird' reads as one phrase; split it after 'game'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a historical trick-taking card pastime and a Eurasian wading sandpiper with showy neck feathers.

clue.text: It doesn't strike a chord all at once

definitions.text: It doesn't strike a chord all at once

blocks.clueFragment: It doesn't strike a chord all at once
blocks.note: surface reading: something that does not immediately resonate or seem familiar
setter's reading: literally play the notes of a chord, but one after another rather than together

explanation.surface: An idea that does not ring a bell straight away.
explanation.definitionFit: This musical term means a broken chord whose notes are played in succession, as on a harp.

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters before it are put back in a fresh arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A celebrity was frustrated at being thrown out of somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turfed out' looks like a single phrase meaning ejected; 'out' is the anagram signal on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone whose plans are blocked or foiled is left disappointed and annoyed, which is both senses of the word.

clue.text: He takes a great deal of interest

definitions.text: He takes a great deal of interest

blocks.clueFragment: He takes a great deal of interest
blocks.note: surface reading: someone very curious or attentive
setter's reading: money charged on a loan, taken at an extortionate rate

explanation.surface: A description of a keenly engaged, attentive person.
explanation.definitionFit: A moneylender who charges excessive rates on loans collects a lot of interest payments.

blocks.note: first meaning: as a noun, a cut diamond, which slang also calls by this word
second meaning: a hand-held stick that throws off bright sparks

explanation.surface: Praise for a dazzling firework display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brilliant' reads as an adjective; it is the noun for a cut diamond.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a diamond gem, and the name of the hand-held sparking stick children wave on bonfire night.

clue.text: Boswell's work was not so dull

blocks.note: James Boswell wrote the famous Life of Samuel Johnson
less means not so much, to a smaller degree

explanation.surface: A literary verdict that Boswell's biography was not as tedious as claimed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something without animation or vigour is flat and boring, the sense of lacking spirit.

indicators.note: the word reads identically from either end, so it can be taken in either direction

blocks.note: the definition alone; the rest of the clue says the word reads identically from either end

explanation.surface: Road-safety advice: check left and right before crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick furtive glance through a gap is a brief, sly sort of looking.

blocks.note: surface reading: the hot-tempered sibling of some thief called Tom
setter's reading: Tom, the piper's son, who stole a pig in the nursery rhyme; his brother picked a peck of pickled peppers

explanation.surface: Asking about the short-tempered brother of a light-fingered Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Peppery suggests irritable; it really points to the tongue-twister about pickled peppers, whose hero shares a surname with Tom the piper's son.
explanation.definitionFit: The tongue-twister hero who picked a peck of pickled peppers shares the surname of Tom from the pig-stealing rhyme.

clue.text: Gossip has it the green's mown the wrong way

indicators.note: done the wrong way means done incorrectly, so the letters are put in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Village chatter says the green has been cut badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wrong way' sounds like mowing direction; it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who spreads rumours and tittle-tattle is a tattler, which is one meaning of gossip as a noun.

clue.text: Provided I amend it an order is affirmed

indicators.note: putting letters into a new order is the instruction to rearrange those that precede it

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bureaucratic statement: once I've changed it, a regulation is confirmed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amend' looks like the anagram signal; it is part of the fodder, and 'order' does the job.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert or declare firmly is to hold to a position, so affirmed and the past tense here are synonyms.

blocks.note: surface reading: a fan of something showy, or a hanger-on of a flashy person
setter's reading: a lightning flash, which is followed by the rumble

explanation.surface: Someone who chases glitz and showiness.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumbling noise of a storm comes after each lightning strike, so it follows the bright burst.

blocks.note: surface reading: not asked to solve a puzzle
setter's reading: a coarse sieve, so this is something never passed through one

explanation.surface: Someone spared from having to answer a conundrum.
explanation.walkthrough: A riddle is also a large garden sieve for soil or gravel.
explanation.definitionFit: Flour or soil that has not been strained through a sieve is described as not having been riddled.

blocks.note: Di's, the possessive of Di, the short form of Diana
a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: To give a false account of Diana's misdeeds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What Diana did wrong' is read as Di's wrong, and a legal wrong is a tort.
explanation.definitionFit: To twist facts or words into a false shape is to give a misleading account of them.

blocks.note: surface reading: a day for making preserves, or a day of traffic jams
setter's reading: the White Queen's rule in Through the Looking-Glass, jam yesterday and jam the next day, but never jam today

explanation.surface: A day set aside for making preserves.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll the White Queen offers jam every other day, and the promised day never arrives; hence the idiom for a promise never kept.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says the promised treat always comes the following day, which is when the jam is due.

clue.text: Weary cry of a boy sheepminder on finding somewhere to sleep?

blocks.clueFragment: Weary cry of a boy sheepminder on finding somewhere to sleep?
blocks.note: surface reading: a tired shepherd boy exclaiming as he finds a bed
setter's reading: Little Boy Blue, found under the haystack fast asleep, who might greet his bed with a cry of 'Hay, oh!'

explanation.surface: A tired young shepherd sighing with relief as he spots a place to nap.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme, the boy who looks after the sheep is under the haystack fast asleep; the sigh sounds like hailing the hay.
explanation.definitionFit: This old interjection expresses tiredness, boredom or resignation, a sigh of weariness.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone well qualified to provide replies
setter's reading: a man who has been sued in a lawsuit and must reply to the petition

explanation.surface: Someone who seems well fitted to give replies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suited' looks like fitting; it means made the subject of a suit at law. Such a party, especially in a divorce petition, must answer the case.
explanation.definitionFit: The defending party in a lawsuit or divorce petition is the one who replies to the case against them.

clue.text: "O what a noble — is here overthrown" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: "O what a noble — is here overthrown" (Hamlet)

blocks.clueFragment: "O what a noble — is here overthrown"
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of Shakespeare with a gap in it
setter's reading: Ophelia's lament for Hamlet's lost sanity in Act 3, which supplies the missing noun

explanation.walkthrough: Ophelia speaks the line after Hamlet seems to rave at her; the missing word is the intellect she thinks has collapsed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ophelia grieves that Hamlet's intellect and reason, once so fine, now seem to have been destroyed by madness.

clue.text: General who took a rest? That's right

definitions.text: General who took a rest? That's right

blocks.note: surface reading: some army commander who paused for a breather
setter's reading: one who naps, a 'napper', which sounds like the surname of the British general Sir Charles

explanation.surface: Asking about a general who had a lie-down, and confirming it.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Charles, the British general who conquered Sind in 1843, has a surname that suggests someone who naps; 'That's right' simply affirms the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Charles, a famous Victorian British army commander, conquered the Indian province of Sind.

clue.text: Excavation unworthy of a top archaeologist?

blocks.clueFragment: Excavation unworthy of a top archaeologist?
blocks.note: surface reading: a minor dig a leading archaeologist would scorn
setter's reading: an archaeological dig that lies below, which is what the Latin-based phrase literally gives

explanation.surface: A lowly excavation a distinguished archaeologist would turn down.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is short for Latin infra dignitatem, beneath one's dignity; read literally it is a dig down below.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means beneath one's dignity, so something a distinguished person would think demeaning.

blocks.note: first meaning: a cloth of a dull light brown colour
second meaning: an old word for a slattern, an untidy or disreputable woman

explanation.surface: Recommending dowdy fabric for a slovenly woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a dull brownish cloth, and archaically a slatternly woman of loose habits.

definitions.note: a definition by location: the thing is found in a flight of stairs

blocks.note: to pass something is to hand it over
a rail is a marsh bird, like the water rail

explanation.surface: Passing a bird that is flying overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In flight' suggests a bird on the wing; the flight is a flight of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A banister or rail to grip runs alongside a staircase, so it is found in any flight of steps.

indicators.note: mixed-up means confused and jumbled, so the letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone conceding that a nymph is rather confused.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman legend she was a water spirit who counselled King Numa, hence a word for a female adviser.

clue.text: Cutting expression from the Norfolk waterways'?

definitions.text: Cutting expression from the Norfolk waterways'?

blocks.clueFragment: Cutting expression from the Norfolk waterways'?
blocks.note: surface reading: a sarcastic remark heard among the Norfolk boating set
setter's reading: the Broads, a region of lakes and rivers in eastern England, whose word, read with the apostrophe, names a cutting weapon

explanation.surface: A sharp remark heard on the Norfolk rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Norfolk Broads are a network of shallow lakes and rivers in eastern England. The apostrophe makes it the Broads' word.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy sword with a wide blade made for slashing is certainly a cutting weapon.
